statement.p:
Consider the vectors
\wvec_1 = \threevec1{-1}1,\hspace{24pt} \wvec_2 = \threevec1{1}0,\hspace{24pt} \wvec_3 = \threevec1{-1}{-2}.
Verify that this set forms an orthogonal set of 3-dimensional vectors.
Explain why we know that this set of vectors forms a basis for \real^3.
Suppose that \bvec=\threevec24{-4}. Find the weights c_1, c_2, and c_3 that express \bvec as a linear combination \bvec=c_1\wvec_1 + c_2\wvec_2 + c_3\wvec_3
using .
If we multiply a vector \vvec by a positive scalar s, the length of \vvec is also multiplied by s; that is, \len{s\vvec} = s\len{\vvec}.
unit vector Using this observation, find a vector \uvec_1 that is parallel to \wvec_1 and has length 1. Such vectors are called unit vectors.
Similarly, find a unit vector \uvec_2 that is parallel to \wvec_2 and a unit vector \uvec_3 that is parallel to \wvec_3.
Construct the matrix Q=\begin{bmatrix} \uvec_1 \amp \uvec_2 \amp \uvec_3 \end{bmatrix} and find the product Q^TQ. Use
to explain your result.

li.p: We compute the dot products \wvec_1\cdot\wvec_2=0, \wvec_1\cdot\wvec_3=0, and \wvec_2\cdot\wvec_3=0.
We know that an orthogonal set of vectors is linearly independent. Therefore, we have a set of three linearly independent vectors in \real^3 so they must form a basis for \real^3.
We find Q^TQ=I since each entry in this matrix product is the dot product of two columns of Q.
We compute the dot products \wvec_1\cdot\wvec_2=0, \wvec_1\cdot\wvec_3=0, and \wvec_2\cdot\wvec_3=0.
An orthogonal set of vectors is linearly independent.
